public_rationale: The closest experiment supports a learning cost from passive delegation, but the claim is stronger: no learning and no improvement. Lower quiz scores do not demonstrate either absolute. Participants who generated code and then studied it showed stronger comprehension, although that subgroup comparison does not establish causation. The evidence therefore supports the concern without settling the categorical claim.
limitations: One short task using an unfamiliar Python library does not represent a software-engineering career.
The available study measures immediate comprehension.
The occupational label 'developing code' is partly definitional.

our_interpretation: The empirical core is that delegating all code authorship prevents learning and improvement attributable to that activity.
Learning means gains in independent programming knowledge, comprehension, debugging or engineering performance; completing work faster is not sufficient.
The surrounding discussion emphasizes passive acceptance of generated code. The sentence itself does not explicitly exclude users who study or test the generated code.
Whether someone remains a developer is partly a definition of the occupation, not a measurable learning outcome.
This is a general causal claim, not a forecast with a dated deadline.
criteria.support_condition: Studies directly examining complete delegation show no learning or engineering-skill improvement attributable to the activity, with evidence sufficiently broad to support the categorical wording.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Credible evidence establishes learning or improved independent engineering ability caused by an activity in which the LLM authors all the code.

evidence.explanation: Two participants who generated code and then sought explanations showed stronger comprehension, while passive delegation was associated with poorer results. The authors say these subgroup associations are not causal findings and that immediate quiz results do not settle long-term development.
